<backstage_guidance>
The induction is finished. Recent passages keep proving that the loan cupboard is locked, permissions are observed, and nobody is imposing on Rowan. Those facts are already secure. Maintain them as background; spend words on them again only when something changes or they affect a present choice. The narrator should describe what happens, without explaining how it respects Rowan's boundaries or what an absent demand means.

Work can remain work. Select details for their particular interest and what they let us experience, rather than recording every safe handling step. A requested time skip should reach its endpoint; a live exchange should leave room for a reply. Do not compensate for a quiet morning by arranging a compulsory encounter or a new problem.

The early supper gave nearly everyone polished rejoinders; the induction then made Nell an instruction manual. Let speech follow the speaker's immediate purpose and relationship with the listener. Plain answers, unfinished exchanges, particular pleasures and unreturned jokes can carry distinct voices. Do not explain the psychology afterwards. A refusal can be accepted without making its acceptance a speech.

There is no need to repair compatible invented details or recite these corrections in the fiction. Keep the established knowledge boundaries, ownership of player choices and real consequences.
</backstage_guidance>

Return the next passage of fiction.

At lunch, if Bea is present, I ask what she enjoys about having the cinema open again. If she is not here, I eat with whoever is around.
</user>

item.text:
At half past twelve, Bea is at one of the cafe tables with Nell, a bank statement and a folder of cinema invoices spread between them. Jo occupies the end nearest the counter, working through supplier prices beside a mug of black coffee.

You bring your lunch over and take the empty chair. The accounts papers are put aside while people eat.

“What do you enjoy about having the cinema open again?” you ask Bea.

She considers this while unwrapping the other half of her sandwich.

“We aren’t open yet, so I may be tempting fate. But I want to see the sign lit. I approved more money for that restoration than a treasurer ought to admit over lunch.”

Nell continues eating without rescuing her from the admission.

“I used to see it from the top deck of the bus after an evening shift,” Bea says. “Then for years it was just a dark shape over an empty building.”

She folds the sandwich paper into a smaller square.

“Mostly, I’m looking forward to somebody coming in who hasn’t attended a fundraiser and doesn’t know any of the trustees. They’ll buy a ticket, choose a seat and perhaps complain that the trailers are too loud. My mother cleaned here and I worked the aisles. It was never important every minute of the day. It was just somewhere people used.”

After a sip of water, she adds, “My granddaughter is coming in October. We send each other appalling films on old discs, so we’ve agreed to choose whatever looks most ill-advised on the programme. She’s forbidden me from giving her a historical tour while we watch it.”
